name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: An AI Gateway and Python SDK for Routing LLM Traffic
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway and Python SDK from BerriAI that lets you call over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It sits between your application and providers such as Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM. The one thing to know before adopting it is that the project is mid-migration from a Python proxy to a Rust core, so performance and stability differ sharply between versions.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and published at github.com/BerriAI/litellm under a custom licence, with a Python SDK and a proxy server that the site describes as the fastest, litest AI Gateway. It sits in the gateway layer of the AI stack, between application code and model providers, translating requests into OpenAI or native formats and returning responses. The repository shows a last push in October 2026 and roughly 60,000 stars. The official documentation is at docs.litellm.ai. The site says the project is moving its core to Rust, with a pure Rust server planned that can serve all AI traffic, including auth and rate limiting, on the hot path.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The gateway routes LLM traffic and applies budgets and rate limits, while the Agent Gateway authenticates callers, controls which users and teams can invoke each agent, and records request, response, latency and cost data. An MCP Gateway centralizes tool access and upstream authentication, including per-user OAuth with PKCE sign-in. The site documents reliability testing across providers, load testing, spend tracking, guardrails, SSO and SAML, audit logs and multi-team management. It is strongest where many providers, teams and budgets must be governed through one control plane, and where per-user and per-agent cost attribution matters. The Rust gateway is presented as the fastest option for coding agents and high-throughput serving.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for developers who already know Python and HTTP APIs, since calls follow OpenAI-style conventions. The gateway side assumes more: you need to understand proxies, Redis, rate limiting, authentication and deployment, because the documented incidents involve Redis outages, retry behaviour and Kubernetes OOM kills. The site offers tutorials, including one on testing multiple providers, and notes quirks such as load_test_model always returning calls_made of 100 regardless of num_calls, and having no interval or duration options. No formal prerequisites in mathematics or systems work are stated, and the documentation does not describe a structured beginner curriculum.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The site lists integrations with Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, and the SDK speaks OpenAI or native formats across more than 100 LLM APIs. The blog covers an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway, an A2A JSON-RPC interface for invoking shared agents, LiteAdmin MCP for management through an agent, and a Slack admin agent built on the same connector. Documentation is extensive, with tutorials, incident reports and benchmark write-ups. Community scale is suggested by the star count, though the facts here do not describe forums, chat channels or contributor numbers.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM serves both ends. The Python SDK and proxy make quick experiments easy, and the site shows batch completion across many models in parallel for reliability testing. Production use is the larger story: the Python proxy peaks around 359MB of memory under load, and the site reports pods being OOM-killed at the worst time. The Rust gateway is claimed to serve about 15 times the throughput, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11 times less memory, 359MB to 32MB, cutting per-request overhead from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. Those figures come from the project's own benchmark, so treat them as vendor measurements rather than independent results.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site describes enterprise customers running the proxy behind nginx, enterprise plans with SSO and SAML, audit logs and multi-team management, and teams sharing agents across business units. It reports an enterprise customer outage with thousands of HTTP 502s and tens of thousands of HTTP 499s, which indicates real production dependence. The project is a current standard in the LLM gateway category rather than a legacy choice, and it is actively changing, with a Rust migration under way. For someone choosing what to learn, gateway and routing skills transfer across providers, but the facts here do not give adoption numbers, customer names or job market data.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is written in Python with a Rust core being introduced, and it is typically used alongside provider SDKs and HTTP clients rather than replacing them. The site says it calls Mistral's API directly over HTTP via httpx and does not import the mistralai Python SDK anywhere, which is the pattern it follows for providers generally. It sits beside frameworks that build agents and applications, handling routing, budgets, guardrails and logging for them, and it exposes an A2A JSON-RPC interface so agents can call each other through the gateway. This is the polyglot gateway pattern: application code in one language, gateway in another, providers behind a common format.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The documented incidents are the clearest limits. A one-line change caused retry breadcrumbs to double in size with every retry, and with Redis unreachable a single allocation reached 27GB, causing kernel OOM kills and a production outage for one customer. A separate regression silently broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock, dropping cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25-45% and raising daily spend two to three times, with no error surfaced. The site also notes that server-side Claude Code auto mode depends on a contract some gateways, LiteLLM included, did not preserve. The Rust gateway is an early beta, the licence is custom rather than a standard open source licence, and the official material does not state independent benchmark results, long-term support commitments or the full scope of the Rust migration timeline.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
